Sign Patterns in a Two Colored Partition Companion series

Aritram Dhar Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL 32611, USA Email address: aritramdhar@ufl.edu, aritramdhar@gmail.com , Ankush Goswami Address: School of Mathematical and Statistical Sciences, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, Edinburg, TX 78541, USA Email address: ankushgoswami3@gmail.com, ankush.goswami@utrgv.edu and Mohit Tripathi Address: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX 79410, USA Email address: mohit.tripathi@ttu.edu
Abstract.

We study three closely related questions arising from the recent work of Andrews and El Bachraoui on the two-color partition series

S1​(q)=∑n≥0s1​(n)​qn=∑a≥0qa​(−qa+1,q)∞2S_{1}(q)=\sum_{n\geq 0}s_{1}(n)q^{n}=\sum_{a\geq 0}q^{a}(-q^{a+1};q)_{\infty}^{2}

and its odd companion, denoted by To​(q)T_{o}(q). First, for the eta-normalized companion

C⁡(q)=(q,q)∞​To​(q)=∑n≥0c⁡(n)​qn,C(q)=(q;q)_{\infty}T_{o}(q)=\sum_{n\geq 0}c(n)q^{n},

we prove a strong form of the Andrews–El Bachraoui sign conjecture that lim supc⁡(n)=+∞\limsup c(n)=+\infty and lim infc⁡(n)=−∞\liminf c(n)=-\infty. Second, we construct an involution using the Franklin-type involution of Chen and Liu to combinatorially explain Andrews–El Bachraoui congruence for s1​(n)s_{1}(n) modulo 4. Third, we introduce a two-variable refinement of S1​(q)S_{1}(q) which records the difference of the lengths of the two colored components. Using Ramanujan’s partial theta identity and heat-type equations, we obtain a closed formula for all of its even moments, and we show that the eta-normalized moments satisfy termwise congruences modulo p2​kp^{2k} for every prime p≡5(mod6)p\equiv 5\pmod{6}.

Key words and phrases: 
two-color partitions; partial theta functions; sign-reversing involutions; moments; heat equations; congruences; quadratic forms
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
05A17, 11P81, 11P83, 11F27

1. Introduction

Throughout the paper, we assume |q|<1|q|<1 and use the standard notation

(a,q)n:=∏j=0n−1(1−a​qj),(a,q)∞:=∏j=0∞(1−a​qj),(a;q)_{n}:=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(1-aq^{j}),\qquad(a;q)_{\infty}:=\prod_{j=0}^{\infty}(1-aq^{j}),

for the qq-Pochhammer symbol, together with the shorthand (a,b,q)∞:=(a,q)∞​(b,q)∞(a,b;q)_{\infty}:=(a;q)_{\infty}(b;q)_{\infty}. We refer to Andrews’ text [2] and to Gasper–Rahman [9] for background on qq-series notation and transformations. Partial theta functions and especially identities of Ramanujan–Andrews type, have long been connected with signed partition identities, false theta phenomena, and Franklin-type cancellations; see, for instance, Alladi, Warnaar, and Andrews–Berndt [1, 4, 13].

Recently, Andrews and El Bachraoui [3] introduced the two-color partition series

(1.1) S1​(q):=∑n≥0s1​(n)​qn=∑a≥0qa​(−qa+1,q)∞2.S_{1}(q):=\sum_{n\geq 0}s_{1}(n)q^{n}=\sum_{a\geq 0}q^{a}(-q^{a+1};q)_{\infty}^{2}.

Combinatorially, s1​(n)s_{1}(n) counts two-color partitions of nn into distinct parts in which the smallest part occurs in one prescribed color, while every larger part may occur in either color or in both colors [3]. Andrews and El Bachraoui proved the following complete modulo 44 description.

Theorem 1 (Andrews–El Bachraoui).

For every n≥0n\geq 0,

s1​(n)≡{(−1)r(mod4),if ​n=r⁡(r+1)/2​ for some ​r≥0,0(mod4),otherwise.s_{1}(n)\equiv\begin{cases}(-1)^{r}\pmod{4},&\text{if }n=r(r+1)/2\text{ for some }r\geq 0,\\ 0\pmod{4},&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

In particular, s1​(n)s_{1}(n) is odd if and only if nn is a triangular number.

They also introduced the odd companion

(1.2) To​(q):=∑n≥0to​(n)​qn=∑m≥0q2​m​(−q,q)2​m(q,q2)m+1,T_{o}(q):=\sum_{n\geq 0}t_{o}(n)q^{n}=\sum_{m\geq 0}\frac{q^{2m}(-q;q)_{2m}}{(q;q^{2})_{m+1}},

and the eta-normalized companion

(1.3) C⁡(q):=∑n≥0c⁡(n)​qn=(q,q)∞​To​(q).C(q):=\sum_{n\geq 0}c(n)q^{n}=(q;q)_{\infty}T_{o}(q).

One of the striking features of these series is that S1​(q)S_{1}(q), To​(q)T_{o}(q), and C⁡(q)C(q) are tied together by partial-theta decompositions and theta-product normalizations. In particular, Andrews and El Bachraoui proved the exact relation

(1.4) S1​(q)=Θ⁡(q)+4​q​To​(q),Θ⁡(q):=∑r≥0(−1)r​qr⁡(r+1)/2.S_{1}(q)=\Theta(q)+4qT_{o}(q),\qquad\Theta(q):=\sum_{r\geq 0}(-1)^{r}q^{r(r+1)/2}.

Thus, away from triangular indices, the congruence of s1​(n)s_{1}(n) modulo 88 is exactly the parity question for To​(q)T_{o}(q). Andrews and El Bachraoui also proved the following sign relations for the coefficients of C⁡(q)C(q) [3].

Theorem 2 (Andrews–El Bachraoui).

For all n≥0n\geq 0,

c⁡(25​n+8)=c⁡(25​n+13)=c⁡(25​n+18)=c⁡(25​n+23)=0,c(25n+8)=c(25n+13)=c(25n+18)=c(25n+23)=0,

and

c⁡(25​n+28)=−c⁡(n).c(25n+28)=-c(n).

In particular, c⁡(n)c(n) changes sign infinitely often and assumes both positive and negative values infinitely often.

At the end of their paper, Andrews and El Bachraoui proposed the following conjecture [3].

Conjecture 1 (Andrews–El Bachraoui).

We have

lim supn→∞c⁡(n)=+∞,lim infn→∞c⁡(n)=−∞.\limsup_{n\to\infty}c(n)=+\infty,\qquad\liminf_{n\to\infty}c(n)=-\infty.

Our first main result is the following stronger statement.

Theorem 3.

For every integer k≥0k\geq 0, there are infinitely many integers nn such that c⁡(n)=2kc(n)=2^{k}, and infinitely many integers nn such that c⁡(n)=−2kc(n)=-2^{k}. In particular,

lim supn→∞c⁡(n)=+∞,lim infn→∞c⁡(n)=−∞.\limsup_{n\to\infty}c(n)=+\infty,\qquad\liminf_{n\to\infty}c(n)=-\infty.

The second theme of the paper concerns combinatorial proof of Theorem 1, thereby answering Problem 2 in [3].

Theorem 4.

Theorem 1 admits a signed involutive proof.

Remark 1.

We note here that Andrews and El Bachraoui also conjectured a congruence for s1​(n)s_{1}(n) modulo 8 [3, Conjecture 2]. This has now been proved by Liu–Xia [12] and, independently, by Banerjee–Bringmann [6].

The third theme of the paper is a two-variable refinement of S1​(q)S_{1}(q). Define

(1.5) 𝒱⁡(z,q):=∑a≥0qa​(−z​qa+1,q)∞​(−z−1​qa+1,q)∞=∑n≥0∑m∈ℤN⁡(m,n)​zm​qn.\mathcal{V}(z;q):=\sum_{a\geq 0}q^{a}(-zq^{a+1};q)_{\infty}(-z^{-1}q^{a+1};q)_{\infty}=\sum_{n\geq 0}\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}N(m,n)z^{m}q^{n}.

Combinatorially, N⁡(m,n)N(m,n) counts triples (a,λ,μ)(a;\lambda,\mu), where a≥0a\geq 0 and the partitions λ\lambda and μ\mu have distinct parts larger than aa, such that

a+|λ|+|μ|=n,ℓ⁡(λ)−ℓ⁡(μ)=m.a+|\lambda|+|\mu|=n,\qquad\ell(\lambda)-\ell(\mu)=m.

Here ℓ⁡(⋅)\ell(\cdot) denotes the number of parts. Clearly 𝒱​(1,q)=S1​(q)\mathcal{V}(1;q)=S_{1}(q), so that s1​(n)=∑mN⁡(m,n)s_{1}(n)=\sum_{m}N(m,n), and ℓ⁡(λ)−ℓ⁡(μ)\ell(\lambda)-\ell(\mu) is a rank-type statistic on the objects counted by s1​(n)s_{1}(n). Interchanging λ\lambda and μ\mu gives N⁡(m,n)=N⁡(−m,n)N(m,n)=N(-m,n). Hence all odd moments vanish. For k≥0k\geq 0, put

(1.6) M2​k​(n):=∑m∈ℤm2​k​N​(m,n),ℳ2​k​(q):=∑n≥0M2​k​(n)​qn,M_{2k}(n):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}m^{2k}N(m,n),\qquad\mathcal{M}_{2k}(q):=\sum_{n\geq 0}M_{2k}(n)q^{n},

in analogy with the rank moments of Atkin and Garvan [5]. In Section 4 we show that Ramanujan’s partial theta identity splits 𝒱⁡(z,q)\mathcal{V}(z;q) into a theta product times a partial theta function, minus a second partial theta function, and that each piece satisfies a heat-type equation. This yields a closed formula for every ℳ2​k​(q)\mathcal{M}_{2k}(q) (Theorem 6). For instance, with δ:=q​dd​q\delta:=q\,\frac{d}{dq}, q=e2​π​i​τq=e^{2\pi i\tau}, and E2​(τ)=1−24​∑n≥1σ1​(n)​qnE_{2}(\tau)=1-24\sum_{n\geq 1}\sigma_{1}(n)q^{n},

ℳ2=6​δ​S1+ℰ​S1−2​δ​Θ+(ℰ−1)​Θ,ℰ=5​E2​(τ)−8​E2​(2​τ)+912.\mathcal{M}_{2}=6\delta S_{1}+\mathcal{E}S_{1}-2\delta\Theta+(\mathcal{E}-1)\Theta,\qquad\mathcal{E}=\frac{5E_{2}(\tau)-8E_{2}(2\tau)+9}{12}.

Our final main result shows that, after multiplication by (q,q)∞(q;q)_{\infty}, the moments are governed by the binary quadratic form x2+3​y2x^{2}+3y^{2}, which is the same form that controls c⁡(n)c(n) in Section 2. Define integers d2​k​(n)d_{2k}(n) by

(1.7) (q,q)∞​ℳ2​k​(q)=:∑n≥0d2​k​(n)​qn,(q;q)_{\infty}\mathcal{M}_{2k}(q)=:\sum_{n\geq 0}d_{2k}(n)q^{n},

and let vpv_{p} denote the pp-adic valuation.

Theorem 5.

Let k≥1k\geq 1, and let p≡5(mod6)p\equiv 5\pmod{6} be prime. Then

d2​k​(n)​{=0if ​vp​(6​n+1)​ is odd,≡0(modp2​k​a)if ​vp​(6​n+1)=2​a.d_{2k}(n)\begin{cases}=0&\text{if }v_{p}(6n+1)\text{ is odd},\\ \equiv 0\pmod{p^{2ka}}&\text{if }v_{p}(6n+1)=2a.\end{cases}

In particular,

(1.8) d2​k​(p​n+5​p−16)≡0(modp2​k).d_{2k}\!\left(pn+\frac{5p-1}{6}\right)\equiv 0\pmod{p^{2k}}.

For example, d2​(5​n+4)≡0(mod25)d_{2}(5n+4)\equiv 0\pmod{25}, d4​(5​n+4)≡0(mod625)d_{4}(5n+4)\equiv 0\pmod{625}, and d2​(11​n+9)≡0(mod121)d_{2}(11n+9)\equiv 0\pmod{121}. The vanishing part of the argument also applies when k=0k=0, and in that case it recovers, and extends to every prime p≡5(mod6)p\equiv 5\pmod{6}, the vanishing statements of Theorem 2; see Corollary 1.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we prove Theorem 3. In Section 3, we give the combinatorial interpretations of the modulo 44 congruence for s1​(n)s_{1}(n), thereby proving Theorem 4. In Section 4, we study the refinement 𝒱⁡(z,q)\mathcal{V}(z;q): we establish its partial theta decomposition, prove the moment formula (Theorem 6) and Theorem 5, and record two special values. We conclude with some open questions in Section 5.

2. Proof of Theorem 3

We use the signed representation formula for c⁡(n)c(n). Put D=6​n+7D=6n+7. Then c⁡(n)c(n) is a signed count of positive solutions of

x2+3​y2=4​D.x^{2}+3y^{2}=4D.

More precisely,

(2.1) c⁡(n)=R1,3​(D)−R5,3​(D)+R7,1​(D)−R11,1​(D),c(n)=R_{1,3}(D)-R_{5,3}(D)+R_{7,1}(D)-R_{11,1}(D),

where Ra,b​(D)R_{a,b}(D) counts positive integer solutions of x2+3​y2=4​Dx^{2}+3y^{2}=4D with x≡a(mod12),y≡b(mod4)x\equiv a\pmod{12},\,y\equiv b\pmod{4}. Thus the residue classes (1,3),(7,1)(1,3),\,(7,1) contribute with plus sign, while (5,3),(11,1)(5,3),\,(11,1) contribute with minus sign. We begin with the elementary representation

28=12+3⋅32.28=1^{2}+3\cdot 3^{2}.

This corresponds to D=7D=7, and the pair (x,y)=(1,3)(x,y)=(1,3) lies in the plus class

(x,y)≡(1,3)(mod(12,4)).(x,y)\equiv(1,3)\pmod{(12,4)}.

Now choose primes pj=uj2+3​vj2p_{j}=u_{j}^{2}+3v_{j}^{2} with uj≡1(mod12),vj≡0(mod4)u_{j}\equiv 1\pmod{12},\,v_{j}\equiv 0\pmod{4}, and with vj/ujv_{j}/u_{j} very small. More precisely, choose positive numbers εj\varepsilon_{j} such that

∑j=1∞εj<η,\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\varepsilon_{j}<\eta,

where η>0\eta>0 is chosen small enough so that rotating either of the two first-quadrant representations of 28=x2+3​y228=x^{2}+3y^{2} by any angle of size less than η\eta keeps it in the first quadrant, and rotating any of the other sign choices by an angle of size less than η\eta keeps it outside the first quadrant. By Hecke’s prime theorem for Grössencharacters, equivalently the prime-ideal theorem in sectors with ray-class conditions [11, Ch. XV, Thm. 6 and Example 2] (see also Hecke’s original formula [10, p. 38, Eq. (52)]), applied in ℤ⁡[−3]\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-3}], every fixed sector 0<arg⁡(u+−3​v)<ε0<\arg(u+\sqrt{-3}v)<\varepsilon contains infinitely many prime elements, we may choose infinitely many distinct primes pjp_{j} satisfying the congruences above and 0<arctan⁡(3​vjuj)<εj.0<\arctan\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}\,v_{j}}{u_{j}}\right)<\varepsilon_{j}. For a fixed kk, define

Dk=7p1p2⋯pk,nk=Dk−76.D_{k}=7p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{k},\qquad n_{k}=\frac{D_{k}-7}{6}.

Since each pj≡1(mod6)p_{j}\equiv 1\pmod{6}, we have Dk≡7(mod6)D_{k}\equiv 7\pmod{6}, so nkn_{k} is an integer. The reason these primes are useful is the multiplication identity

(x2+3​y2)​(u2+3​v2)=(x​u−3​y​v)2+3​(x​v+y​u)2=(x​u+3​y​v)2+3​(y​u−x​v)2,(x^{2}+3y^{2})(u^{2}+3v^{2})=(xu-3yv)^{2}+3(xv+yu)^{2}=(xu+3yv)^{2}+3(yu-xv)^{2},

Thus, each time we multiply by one prime pj=uj2+3​vj2p_{j}=u_{j}^{2}+3v_{j}^{2}, we get two possible new representations. Starting from 28=12+3⋅3228=1^{2}+3\cdot 3^{2} and multiplying successively by p1,p2,…,pkp_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{k}, we obtain 2k2^{k} representations of

x2+3​y2=4​Dk.x^{2}+3y^{2}=4D_{k}.

We now check that all these 2k2^{k} representations are counted with plus sign. Suppose a representation lies in the class

(x,y)≡(1,3)(mod(12,4)).(x,y)\equiv(1,3)\pmod{(12,4)}.

Using

uj≡1(mod12),vj≡0(mod4),u_{j}\equiv 1\pmod{12},\qquad v_{j}\equiv 0\pmod{4},

we see from the two multiplication formulas that the new xx-coordinate is still congruent to 1(mod12)1\pmod{12}, and the new yy-coordinate is still congruent to 3(mod4)3\pmod{4}. Hence both choices preserve the class (1,3)(1,3). Therefore all 2k2^{k} representations coming from the starting pair (1,3)(1,3) remain in the plus class (1,3)(1,3). The small-angle condition ensures that these representations remain positive. Indeed, the factor uj+−3​vju_{j}+\sqrt{-3}\,v_{j} has angle

arctan⁡(3​vjuj),\arctan\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}\,v_{j}}{u_{j}}\right),

which is smaller than εj\varepsilon_{j}. After kk steps, the total change in direction is at most

ε1+⋯+εk<η.\varepsilon_{1}+\cdots+\varepsilon_{k}<\eta.

By the choice of η\eta, the resulting points still lie in the first quadrant. Thus the corresponding xx and yy remain positive. It remains to explain why the negative classes do not contribute. The other first-quadrant representation of 28=x2+3​y228=x^{2}+3y^{2} is 28=52+3⋅1228=5^{2}+3\cdot 1^{2}. This pair lies in the class

(x,y)≡(5,1)(mod(12,4)),(x,y)\equiv(5,1)\pmod{(12,4)},

which is not one of the four signed classes appearing in the formula (2.1) for c⁡(n)c(n). The same congruence calculation shows that multiplying by any of the primes pjp_{j} preserves this class. Hence all representations generated from (5,1)(5,1) remain uncounted. Finally, the elementary uniqueness theory for representations by x2+3​y2x^{2}+3y^{2} [8] says that, since Dk=7p1p2⋯pkD_{k}=7p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{k} is squarefree and each pjp_{j} is represented by uj2+3​vj2u_{j}^{2}+3v_{j}^{2}, every representation of x2+3​y2=4​Dkx^{2}+3y^{2}=4D_{k} is obtained from one of the representations of 28=x2+3​y228=x^{2}+3y^{2} by making the two choices above at each prime factor, together with possible sign changes. By our choice of η\eta, the sign-changed starting points remain outside the first quadrant after the small rotations, so they do not contribute to the positive-solution count. Consequently, among the four signed classes in the formula for c⁡(n)c(n), only the plus class (1,3)(1,3) contributes. It contributes exactly 2k2^{k} times. Thus

R1,3​(Dk)=2k,R_{1,3}(D_{k})=2^{k},

while

R5,3​(Dk)=R7,1​(Dk)=R11,1​(Dk)=0.R_{5,3}(D_{k})=R_{7,1}(D_{k})=R_{11,1}(D_{k})=0.

Because the primes pjp_{j} can be chosen in infinitely many ways, this gives infinitely many nkn_{k} with c⁡(nk)=2kc(n_{k})=2^{k}. Hence

lim supn→∞c⁡(n)=+∞.\limsup_{n\to\infty}c(n)=+\infty.

The negative direction follows from the known relation c⁡(25​n+28)=−c⁡(n)c(25n+28)=-c(n). Applying this to the sequence nkn_{k}, we get

c⁡(25​nk+28)=−c⁡(nk)=−2k.c(25n_{k}+28)=-c(n_{k})=-2^{k}.

Since kk is arbitrary, this gives

lim infn→∞c⁡(n)=−∞.\liminf_{n\to\infty}c(n)=-\infty.

The result follows.∎

3. Proof of Theorem 4

In this section we give a signed interpretation of the modulo 44 congruence for s1​(n)s_{1}(n). The key point is the following simple identity:

(3.1) (1+qr)2=(1−qr)2+4​qr.(1+q^{r})^{2}=(1-q^{r})^{2}+4q^{r}.

Modulo 44, S1​(q)S_{1}(q) and its signed generating function F⁡(q)F(q) (defined below) are congruent. By constructing an involution on the signed object using a Franklin-type involution of Chen and Liu [7], we show that the fixed points of our involution are triangular-number staircases, proving Theorem 1. Using (1.1) and (3.1), we get

(3.2) S1​(q)≡F⁡(q):=∑a≥0qa​(qa+1,q)∞2(mod4).S_{1}(q)\equiv F(q):=\sum_{a\geq 0}q^{a}(q^{a+1};q)_{\infty}^{2}\pmod{4}.

The right-hand side is the signed generating function for triples X=(a,λ,μ)X=(a;\lambda,\mu), where a≥0a\geq 0 and λ,μ\lambda,\mu are distinct-part partitions with all parts strictly larger than aa. We assign

w⁡(X)=a+|λ|+|μ|,sgn⁡(X)=(−1)ℓ⁡(λ)+ℓ⁡(μ).w(X)=a+|\lambda|+|\mu|,\qquad\operatorname{sgn}(X)=(-1)^{\ell(\lambda)+\ell(\mu)}.

Thus

(3.3) F⁡(q)=∑Xsgn⁡(X)​qw⁡(X).F(q)=\sum_{X}\operatorname{sgn}(X)q^{w(X)}.

These are exactly the triples counted by N⁡(m,n)N(m,n) in (1.5), and since sgn⁡(X)=(−1)ℓ⁡(λ)−ℓ⁡(μ)\operatorname{sgn}(X)=(-1)^{\ell(\lambda)-\ell(\mu)}, we have F⁡(q)=𝒱⁡(−1,q)F(q)=\mathcal{V}(-1;q).

We now describe a complete sign-reversing involution on these triples. Rather than forcing a long case-by-case map directly on (a,λ,μ)(a;\lambda,\mu), we transfer the problem to the distinct-part model used by Chen and Liu in their Franklin-type involution for squares [7]. Define

(3.4) Φ⁡(a,λ,μ)=ρ:={2​a}∪{2​r:r∈λ}∪{2​s−1:s∈μ}.\Phi(a;\lambda,\mu)=\rho:=\{2a\}\cup\{2r:r\in\lambda\}\cup\{2s-1:s\in\mu\}.

Then ρ\rho is a partition into distinct nonnegative parts whose smallest part is even. If o⁡(ρ)o(\rho) denotes the number of odd parts of ρ\rho, then

(3.5) |ρ|+o⁡(ρ)=2​w​(a,λ,μ),|\rho|+o(\rho)=2w(a;\lambda,\mu),

and

(3.6) (−1)ℓ⁡(ρ)−1=(−1)ℓ⁡(λ)+ℓ⁡(μ).(-1)^{\ell(\rho)-1}=(-1)^{\ell(\lambda)+\ell(\mu)}.

Therefore F⁡(q)F(q) is the weighted signed generating function of distinct nonnegative partitions with smallest part even.

Chen and Liu [7, Theorem 5.1] constructed an explicit Franklin-type involution on precisely such distinct-part partitions ρ\rho. Denote their involution by ψ\psi. It preserves the statistics |ρ||\rho|, and their proof confirms that the involution also preserves o⁡(ρ)o(\rho), and hence, w⁡(a,λ,μ)=(|ρ|+o⁡(ρ))/2w(a;\lambda,\mu)=(|\rho|+o(\rho))/2; reverses the parity of ℓ⁡(ρ)−1\ell(\rho)-1, and has fixed points

(3.7) ρm=(0,1,3,5,…,2​m−1),m≥0.\rho_{m}=(0,1,3,5,\ldots,2m-1),\qquad m\geq 0.

For example, the elementary part of ψ\psi is as follows: if the smallest part of ρ\rho is positive, one inserts a zero part; if the smallest part is 00 and the next smallest part is even, one deletes the zero part. The remaining case, in which the smallest part is 00 and the next smallest part is odd, is handled by the modular hook map of Chen and Liu. We define the composition map

(3.8) ι=Φ−1∘ψ∘Φ.\iota=\Phi^{-1}\circ\psi\circ\Phi.

Noting that Φ\Phi is a bijection, we immediately see that ι\iota is a complete weight-preserving, sign-reversing involution on all triples except the preimages of (3.7). These preimages are exactly

(3.9) Xm=(0,∅,(1,2,…,m)).X_{m}=(0;\varnothing,(1,2,\ldots,m)).

They have

w⁡(Xm)=1+2+⋯+m=m⁡(m+1)2,sgn⁡(Xm)=(−1)m.w(X_{m})=1+2+\cdots+m=\frac{m(m+1)}{2},\qquad\operatorname{sgn}(X_{m})=(-1)^{m}.

Consequently

(3.10) F⁡(q)=∑m≥0(−1)m​qm⁡(m+1)/2.F(q)=\sum_{m\geq 0}(-1)^{m}q^{m(m+1)/2}.

Combining (3.2) and (3.10) proves the result. An independent analytic derivation of (3.10), obtained by specializing the refinement 𝒱⁡(z,q)\mathcal{V}(z;q) at z=−1z=-1, is given in Remark 2 below.

4. Moments of the length-difference statistic

In this section we study the refinement 𝒱⁡(z,q)\mathcal{V}(z;q) defined in (1.5) and its moments (1.6).

4.1. Notation

We write

Dz:=z​∂∂z,δ:=q​∂∂q,D_{z}:=z\frac{\partial}{\partial z},\qquad\delta:=q\frac{\partial}{\partial q},

and recall that Θ⁡(q)=∑r≥0(−1)r​qr⁡(r+1)/2\Theta(q)=\sum_{r\geq 0}(-1)^{r}q^{r(r+1)/2} from (1.4). Let

5. Conclusion

We conclude with a few open questions below.

  1. (1)

    Is there a rank or crank statistic on the signed objects associated with S1​(q)S_{1}(q) that explains the modulo 44 congruence directly? The length difference ℓ⁡(λ)−ℓ⁡(μ)\ell(\lambda)-\ell(\mu) underlying 𝒱⁡(z,q)\mathcal{V}(z;q) is a natural candidate to start from.

  2. (2)

    Prove the Andrews–El Bachraoui modulo 88 congruence [3, Conjecture 2] for s1​(n)s_{1}(n) combinatorially.

  3. (3)

    Do the special values 𝒱⁡(i,q)\mathcal{V}(i;q) and 𝒱⁡(ω,q)\mathcal{V}(\omega;q) admit partial theta decompositions analogous to (4.5), and do they lead to congruences or sign patterns for the corresponding residue-class counts of N⁡(m,n)N(m,n)?
